messages.content:
Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
Below is a high‑level “recipe” for how you could orchestrate those two tools to place a real‑world food order at McDonald’s.  
I’ll walk through each step, what information you’d need, and give a concrete example of the JSON strings you might feed into the *execute* tool once everything else has been found.

---

### Step 1 – Find the right public / partner API

| What we’re looking for | Why it matters |
|------------------------|----------------|
| **McDonald’s official ordering API** (or a third‑party service such as DoorDash, UberEats, Grubhub, etc.) | It will expose endpoints for retrieving menus, adding items to cart, checking out, etc. |
| **Authentication method** (OAuth2 bearer tokens, API keys, signed JWTs, etc.) | You can’t hit protected routes without proper credentials. |
| **Rate limits & usage policies** | Avoid hitting your quota or violating terms of service. |

> **Tool #1 – Search Internet**  
> Call `search_internet("McDonald's online ordering API")`.  
> Parse the results until you locate something like:
>
> ```
> "https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/menu"
> "POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/cart/add"
> "POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/order/place"
> ```

If there isn’t a publicly documented API, look for a **partner integration portal** where restaurants publish their own SDKs or REST contracts.  

---

### Step 2 – Discover the exact item identifiers

Once you have the base URLs, you need the numeric or alphanumeric codes that represent specific menu items (“Big Mac”, “French Fries”). These usually live behind a `/menu` endpoint.

```text
GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/menu?location=12345&format=json
```

Parse the returned JSON tree until you see entries similar to:

```json
[
   {
      "item_id": "BGMK",
      "name": "Big Mac",
      ...
   },
   {
      "item_id": "FRY_LG",
      "name": "Large French Fries",
      ...
   }
]
```

Store `"BGMK"` and `"FRY_LG"` for later use.

---

### Step 3 – Build the shopping‑cart payload

Most modern e‑commerce APIs accept a list of line items. For McDonald’s this typically looks like:

```json
{
   "items":[
       { "productId":"BGMK", "quantity":1},
       { "productId":"FRY_LG", "quantity":1}
   ],
   "deliveryMethod":"pickup",
   "storeLocation":"12345"
}
```

Make sure you also supply any required fields such as store id (`storeLocation`) or delivery address if you’re not picking up.

---

### Step 4 – Authenticate

Depending on the chosen platform you may need to exchange a username/password for a short‑lived access token first:

```http
POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/auth/token
Body: { "client_id":"abc", "client_secret":"xyz", "grant_type":"client_credentials"}
Response: { "access_token":"eyJhb...", "expires_in":3600 }
```

Keep the `access_token` handy because all subsequent calls require it in the `Authorization` header:

```
Authorization: Bearer eyJhb...
```

---

### Step 5 – Execute the add‑to‑cart operation

Now you’re ready to fire off the second tool—“Execute API call”—with the full request string.

#### Example Request String

```python
requests.post(
    url="https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/cart/add",
    headers={
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {ACCESS_TOKEN}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Accept": "application/json"
    },
    json={
        "items":[{"productId":"BGMK","quantity":1},{"productId":"FRY_LG","quantity":1}],
        "deliveryMethod":"pickup",
        "storeLocation":"12345"
    },
    timeout=15
)
```

When you pass this whole block to the execute tool, it will perform the network round‑trip and return whatever status code and body the API gives back (e.g., success confirmation, error messages).

---

### Optional – Place the Order

If the cart addition succeeded, you normally follow up with a checkout endpoint:

```python
requests.post(
    url="https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/order/place",
    headers={ ... same auth … },
    json={"paymentToken":"tok_visa_xxx"},
    timeout=20
)
```

Again, feed the entire string into the execute tool. Once you get a successful response, you’ve effectively ordered a Big Mac + Large Fries!

---

## Recap of Tool Usage Flow

| Stage | Action | Tool Used |
|-------|--------|-----------|
| 1️⃣ Identify API contract | Search web → parse docs | **Search Internet** |
| 2️⃣ Pull menu catalog | GET menu → extract ids | **Search Internet** (for endpoint discovery) |
| 3️⃣ Prepare payload | Assemble JSON objects | None (local prep) |
| 4️⃣ Get auth token | OAuth flow | **Search Internet** (if needed) |
| 5️⃣ Add to cart | POST cart endpoint | **Execute API call** |
| 6️⃣ Checkout | POST order endpoint | **Execute API call** |

That’s essentially the end‑to‑end pipeline: discover → authenticate → build → execute. With the correct endpoints and valid credentials, feeding the fully formed request string into the *execute* tool will do the heavy lifting for you.
